notes.trap: `pmod(...)` is only guaranteed non-negative when the divisor is positive. With a negative divisor it can still return a negative value, because Spark computes r = a % n and, if r < 0, returns (r + n) % n.
`mod(...)` and `%` return a remainder with the sign of the dividend, unlike mathematical modulo. A zero divisor returns NULL instead of raising an error, because ANSI mode is off by default.
`div` truncates toward zero, not toward negative infinity, and always returns BIGINT. A zero divisor gives NULL rather than an error when ANSI mode is off.
Spark's `ln(...)` returns NULL for zero and negative inputs instead of -Infinity or NaN, as Java or other engines would. The logarithm functions `log10(...)` and `log2(...)` behave the same way.

The two-argument form takes the base FIRST: `log(base, expr)`. Some engines put the base second, or treat single-argument log as base 10, whereas Spark's one-argument `log(...)` is the natural log. A non-positive base or value returns NULL, not an error.
`log1p(...)` returns NULL, not -Infinity, when the input is less than or equal to -1.
`factorial(...)` only supports inputs 0..20, the range that fits in a BIGINT. Anything outside that range, including negatives, silently returns NULL rather than an error or a decimal result.
For DOUBLE or FLOAT input, single-argument `floor(...)` returns BIGINT, not a floating type. Decimal input returns a DECIMAL instead, so the result type depends on the input type.
`greatest(...)` and `least(...)` skip NULL arguments and return NULL only if every argument is NULL. Engines such as MySQL or Oracle instead return NULL as soon as any argument is NULL.

For integral input, `hex(...)` formats the value as a 64-bit two's-complement long, so negative numbers produce 16 hex digits instead of a minus sign. For string input it hex-encodes the UTF-8 bytes rather than parsing a number.
With ANSI mode off, `negative(...)` silently overflows for the minimum value of an integral type and returns the same minimum value instead of raising an error.
`csc(...)` is computed as 1/sin(x) in double arithmetic, so csc(0) returns Infinity instead of NULL or an error.
